content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces an unsupervised transformer-based deep learning framework to optimize cell and gene embeddings jointly. The new framework leverages gene names, gene count matrix, and even other external information (such as functional path or perturbation) to obtain better representation embedding at the single-cell level. The representation embedding can benefit downstream tasks like inferring cell types, detecting gene-gene functional relations, and predicting perturbation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Main Review
The main purpose of obtaining the representation of scRNA-seq data is to benefit downstream tasks. The experiments and results section contains three sorts of downstream analysis: cell clustering, batch correction, and perturbation prediction. However, the results so far are far from convincing. 
1. The introduction section and related work mentioned “gene-gene interaction” and “gene-gene functional relations”. It seems that the framework utilized a self-attention mechanism to model the gene relationship. It would be helpful if authors could conduct enough experiments to demonstrate it.
2. In the 4.1 section, the related work section mentioned several works, such as Seurat, LIGER, OCAT, scVI, TotalVI. Why only compare scFormer with HVG, Seurat and scVI? There are merely several tables to demonstrate the performance of cell clustering parts. It would be more convincing if authors could provide figures to visualize it. And the table shows that Seurat performs better than scFormer when using ARI as metric.
3. In section 4.2, it seems that Fig 2(a) is the same as Fig 3(A). Please check it carefully. Fig 3(B) shows that cells of the same type from different batches were not integrated. For instance, alpha cells from inDrop3, inDrop2, celseq2 are not integrated, which is not a single case.
4. In table 3, the ablation results show that scFormer is not the best one in AvgBATCH metrics.
5. In 4.3, There are only two comparative methods. More comparative methods would make the experiments more convincing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The manuscript is not well formulated. The results are not convincing enough. The downstream analysis is too weak to demonstrate the advance of the framework. More experiments need to be conducted to make the paper more convincing, and the comparative methods are insufficient to support the conclusion.

replying_to: Replying to scFormer: a universal representation learning approach for single-cell data using transformers
display_title: Official Review of Paper20 by Reviewer BBct

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a method, called scFormer, for representation learning of single cell RNA-seq data. ScFormer uses gene names as tokens in a transformer architecture and defines three embeddings for genes, cells, and external tokens. The final embedding is the summation of these three embeddings. ScFormer then uses four head tasks after embeddings: 1- masked gene modeling (MGM), 2- masked value for cell modeling (MVC), 3- elastic cell similarity (ECS), and 4- domain adaptation by reverse back-propagation (DAR). The authors ablate the model by removing each part and report that the full model archives the best performance. ScFormer is able to simultaneously address cell-level (such as cell annotation) and gene-level (such as gene-gene interactions and functions) questions. ScFormer is also able to predict the effects of gene perturbations as shown using some Perturb-seq datasets. The authors have shown that scFormer outperforms some of the competing methods in different datasets in terms of both biological conservation metrics as well as batch correction performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

- It is interesting to have a model that is able to model both gene-level and cell-level information and can answer questions for each level.
- The ablation study is helpful to see that both gene-level and cell-level tasks together contribute the most to the model.
- The experimental results are interesting and shows the effectiveness of the model compared to the others (such as scVI) in cell embedding and also perturbation prediction results.

Weakness:

- Based on the ablation results by the authors, the performance of scFormer is very sensitive to the percentage of the masked genes for which the model predicts the expression values.
- The authors use a rather strange normalization of the gene expression values based on binning which does not makes perfect sense.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear and high quality. The novelty is medium: it is new in that they have proposed a model amenable for gene- and cell-level queries. However, the modeling architecture is not very novel.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper proposes an interesting model for representation learning of the scRNA-seq data, where it is possible to share the information across both gene and cell dimensions. It is interesting that the paper shows such integration across both directions works better than other methods that do not use such information sharing. I like the idea and believe that it could be a useful model for addressing both cell-level and gene-level queries. However, I have the following questions/comments:

- Why have the authors binned the expression values rather than working with the expression values as is? Instead of binning and using cross-entropy, one could use the log-transformed value with MSE loss or count values with Poisson loss, etc. I wonder how the model would perform using such loss functions? Also, what is B in the binning? I assume we should decide B and that could also change the model performance?

- Based on ablation, choosing different percentage of masked genes could dramatically change the performance of the model. This sensitivity is not good and can lead the model to a suboptimal performance in an unsupervised dataset where there is no access to cell annotations. What would the authors suggest to choose this percentage such that there is not much drop in the performance?

- What is the value of the embedding dimension D used in the transformers and how much the performance changes based on that?

- How much is the effect of external tokens in the model?

- Have the authors used the set of all expressed genes instead of highly variable genes? I wonder how that could change the performance. 

- How scalable is the model for a larger set of genes, for example, when one uses all the expressed genes instead of highly variable genes? It could be interesting if the authors could report the training time as a function of number of genes.

Minor comments:

- Right before eq (1), it says t_g^(i) \in N^K. Should it be N^M?
- Some typos:
               - a embedding --> an embedding
               - re-procecessed --> re-processed 
               - shows its performance --> show its performance
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

replying_to: Replying to scFormer: a universal representation learning approach for single-cell data using transformers
display_title: Official Review of Paper20 by Reviewer evkH

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors suggest a novel method coined scFormer that leverages a transformer-based architecture to jointly learn embeddings of cells and genes from scRNA-seq data.
Despite being trained in a self-supervised way, the representation learned is used to perform various downstream tasks such as clustering, batch correction and perturbation prediction.
After describing the approach, the authors evaluate the performance of their method on those tasks against some competing methods and perform some ablation studies.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Despite some intriguing premises, I think the current manuscript presents several majors flaws. I will start by addressing the most important ones.
1) Although it is the very core of the premise of the paper, I think the analogy between natural language and gene expression data is not clear at all and I do not understand the intuition behind the gene tokens.
At least within a batch, gene expression data are vectors where the coordinates correspond to genes, and whose order is fixed and mostly arbitrary.
As such, unless I misunderstood the premise, the gene token vectors t_g^(i) will be identical for all the cells within a given batch.
And the absence of any additional information (such as co-occurrence matrices, as used in various methods in the literature), I do not understand what kind of information those vectors will carry.
2) The external tokens sound like an interesting way to leverage this kind of additional information.
However, according to their definition, unless the notations suddenly changed, those tokens, which are supposed to encode information about genes, are indexed by i.
Again, I do not understand why those tokens would not be identical vectors across the different cells of a given batch.
3) In the embedding layers, I understand that the output of the look-up tables will have dimension MxD (although, with regards to my previous comments, it boils down to essentially encode constants).
However, it is not clear how the output of the embedding of x has such dimension as the output of an MLP on a vector of size M.
4) Although the expression values x have been discretized, the MGM and MVC tasks are in essence regression tasks.
It is very counterintuitive to me why a classification loss, such as the cross-entropy should be used there.
5) I fail to understand the "contrastive" nature of the ECS task. Are there positive and negative pairs?
From the description given here, it looks like this loss will enforce that all pairs of cell codes should have a similarity value close to \Beta.
I also do not understand what is meant by disentangling of cell representations in this context.
I also think the reference given (Liu et al. 2019) is wrong as I could not find any reference to such a loss in that paper.
6) Given that an identity transformation from the raw data would yield the best results for the first task, and that it is redundant with the evaluation on the batch correction task, I do not find those results to be very meaningful.
7) The results on the batch correction task highlight the natural trade-off that exists between a good mixing of the cells from different batches and the conservation of the original structure of the data.
Compared to Harmony or scVI, scFormer seems to conserve more of the original structure but to integrate less.
I don't think the claim that biological conservation is the more important metric to be valid. For instance, if you want to integrate batches that have cell type annotation to "transfer" them to the batches that are not annotated, a better mixing is often crucial.
As such, I don't think that those results are conclusive.

It is very possible that at least part of the issues come from misunderstandings on my end.
If those misunderstandings are lifted, I would be very keen on changing my evaluation of this paper.
In any case, I do believe that it reflects at the very least on a lack of clarity of the current manuscript.


Less important (but still important) concerns:
- I find that the clarity is often hindered by a lack of precision. For instance, scRNA-seq is said (in Section 3) to "measure the individual abundance of RNA molecules in each cell". It counts the RNA reads that can be mapped to different genes as a proxy to its expression level.
- A bit further, an entry X_i,j is a count of how many reads mapped to gene j were counted in cell i.
- While, due to some normalization, the entries are often floats, (sc)RNA-seq data are still count matrices, and as such are not really continuous.
- For self-containedness, the definition of the transformer block used in Eq. 6 could be added (at least in the appendices).
- I imagine that in the end, scFormer is trained to minimize a weighted sum of the 3 losses associated to the first task while maximizing the 4th but it would be nice to give more details to improve the clarity and reproducibility.
- There are many more typos or imprecision in the vocabulary used (e.g. Natural Language Modeling instead of NLP, MLM instead of MGM (I think?) in the description of the MVC task...). Please give the paper a careful proof-read before publication.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I think the quality and clarity of the current manuscript is problematic for the different reasons exposed previously.
The originality of the approach should also be more carefully studied. There are definitely a lot of similarities with scBert, for instance, that would call for a deeper analysis (and experimental comparison to).
I did not look deeply into the code provided by the authors, but I believe some more details (such as a precise definition of the loss optimized during training) should be provided to ensure more reproducibility.
(As a side note, the trainer.py file provided in the anonymous repo is empty.)
content.summary_of_the_review:
I believe the suggested model suffers from multiple crucial flaws in its conceptualization, in its evaluation and in the clarity/correctness of the manuscript.
As such, I recommend that this submission be rejected.
As mentioned previously, I am puzzled by many of the points I raised, and opened to the idea that I might have completely misunderstood the foundation of this contribution.
If that is the case, I will be open to revising my evaluation of the paper.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

display_title: Official Review of Paper20 by Reviewer j75F

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work presents a transformer-based method to learn representations for cells and for genes based on scRNA-seq datasets. 

 - $X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times G}$ is the positive cells by genes matrix. Gene names and binned expression values are assigned tokens, which are mapped and aggregated into a learnable $D$ dimensional embedding. 
 - Transformer blocks (stacked) process the $\mathbb{R}^{D \times G}$ embeddings with an appended `<cls>` token. Output of the last transformer block provides the gene representations, and the cell representation is read out from the position of the `<cls>` token. 
 - To train this model (and associated task heads), the loss terms from two imputation task (Masked gene modeling, and masked cell modeling), a contrastive learning term for the cell representation, and a domain adaptation term from are jointly optimized.

Results:
 - The cell representations are clustered, and the resulting clusters are shown to overlap well with ground truth labels while ignoring known technical noise (Tables 1 and 2). This suggests that the method works, and learns interpretable representations.
 - Gene representations show that marker genes corresponding to distinct cell types appear clustered accordingly
 - Ablation results suggest that the imputation tasks are crucial for training the model effectively. 
 - Results on perturbation prediction tasks is competitive.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
 - The paper is generally easy to read
 - The work opens possibility to incorporate metadata about genes in such analyses
 - Perturbation study and performance on that task is interesting

Weakness:
 - The evaluation lacks error bars, and has too narrow a focus (expanded upon in other sections of the review)
 - Gene representations are under-explored
 - Perturbation experiments are under-reported/ under explored
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and Quality:
 - Overall a clearly written manuscript
 - Figures have symbols too small to read

Novelty:
 - Transformers have been applied to tabular data (e.g. [Gorishniy et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.11959v2.pdf)). All the loss terms (completion tasks, domain adaptation term, contrastive term) seem to be well known. 
 - Others (e.g. [Vargo et al. 2020](https://bmcbioinformatics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12859-020-03641-z)) have considered rank-based analysis of gene expression data (referred to as value binning in this work here).

Reproducibility:
 - Datasets, evaluation methodology needs to be documented better.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Major

 1. It is unclear what motivates use of the transformer architecture. There is no sequence structure, it is possible to load the entire dataset at once since the authors only showcase experiments with restricted gene sets, and learned gene representations do not seem to reveal much (other than clustering of marker genes according to cell types - which is a straightforward consequence of how marker genes are defined). There isn't a demonstration for external tokens either (in other words the flexibility to incorporate gene metadata).
 2. The clustering methodology is not detailed in the paper, and is central to the results showing better agreement with ground truth labels than other approaches (Table 1). The choice of metric, clustering algorithm, hyperparameters etc. are all crucial to the performance reported. Error bars are missing from all of the reported quantitative numbers - either arising from random initializations, or from cross validation sets etc. 
3. In my opinion, it would be more compelling to compare scFormer with equivalent non-transformer baseline architectures (e.g. MLP trained with similar loss terms as the scFormer model is) and do a more detailed analysis on one or two datasets for biological interpretation rather than going after "state of the art" performance on cell representations on a miscellaneous collection of datasets. Challenges in tuning competing methods, noisy ground truth, unequal evaluation procedures, make is really difficult to say something reliable about new methods based only on narrow metrics. 

Minor

 - "External tokens" are never showcased to have any utility
 - The assertion that "value binning" has "consistent semantic meaning across cells" is unfounded due to technical noise in the data.
 - While the authors claim that genes can be dynamically subsampled, they do not perform experiments with this. I think demonstrating this could be useful (e.g. in predicting cell types where a far fewer number of genes are measured compared to reference datasets e.g. spatial transcriptomics experiments)
 - As the authors point out, the analogy with NLP breaks down because only gene names are considered which are permutation invariant. Perhaps the authors could use nucleotide sequences that are associated with the genes (e.g. see Enformer, Avsec et al. 2021). 
 - For Eq. 7 and 8, it is not clear why the cross entropy loss is used, given that the gene expression values are clearly ordered. I understand that claim is that "value binning" is a "semantic" understanding of the gene expression value, but I find this to be puzzling nevertheless. 
 - I'd love to see a more insightful result with gene representations. The sanity check with marker genes is somewhat underwhelming mostly because it's a very salient feature - by definition marker genes are robustly "on" only for particular cell types (and "off" otherwise), even a simple correlation based analysis would group marker genes together.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
